A.explanation: One full cycle occupies $4 \text{ cm}$ and has period $0.4 \text{ ms}$, so time-base is $0.4/4 = 0.1 \text{ ms cm}^{-1}$.

B.explanation: This uses $0.4 \text{ ms}$ for $1 \text{ cm}$ instead of for the full $4 \text{ cm}$ wavelength seen peak-to-peak.

C.explanation: This has the correct numbers but uses seconds, which is 1000 times too large for a $2.5 \text{ kHz}$ wave.

D.explanation: This confuses the $0.4 \text{ ms}$ period with the time-base and also uses seconds instead of milliseconds.

hints: Count the horizontal length of one complete sine wave on the $1 \text{ cm}$ grid by measuring peak-to-peak distance.
Convert the given $2.5 \text{ kHz}$ frequency to period using $T = 1/f$ in milliseconds.
Divide that period by the number of centimetres in one cycle to get time per centimetre.
walkthrough: Measure one wavelength on the CRO screen. From one peak to the next peak is $4$ squares of $1 \text{ cm}$, so one cycle is $4 \text{ cm}$ wide.
State the period rule $T = 1/f$. Here $f = 2.5 \text{ kHz} = 2500 \text{ Hz}$.
Substitute: $T = 1/2500 = 0.0004 \text{ s} = 0.4 \text{ ms}$. This is the time for one $4 \text{ cm}$ cycle.
Calculate the time-base: $\text{time-base} = \text{time per cycle} / \text{cm per cycle} = 0.4 \text{ ms} / 4 \text{ cm} = 0.1 \text{ ms cm}^{-1}$.
